title: Edge & DNS
oneLiner: Route 53 decides which IP. CloudFront caches and speeds up HTTP. Global Accelerator is a fast on-ramp for any TCP/UDP, with static IPs and failover that doesn't wait on DNS.

notes.html: Every question about these three comes down to four checks: is it HTTP?, does it need caching?, does it need static IPs?, and how fast must failover be?

notes.caption: Where each service sits in one request

head: Route 53
CloudFront
Global Accelerator
rows: DNS TTL, and clients may cache longer

items: "Dynamic content" does not rule out CloudFront. With TTL 0 it still terminates TLS at the edge and rides the backbone to the origin. Rule it out only for non-HTTP traffic or a static-IP requirement.
Global Accelerator handles HTTPS fine. HTTPS runs on TCP. GA just doesn't look inside it or cache it.
Mobile apps cache DNS. So Route 53 weighted blue/green shifts slowly for them. GA swaps endpoints (traffic dials, endpoint weights) without DNS changes.
CloudFront origin failover only retries GET, HEAD and OPTIONS. An API that takes POSTs needs GA or Route 53 for regional failover.
They stack. Route 53 → CloudFront → ALB is a normal answer. Read what the question actually constrains.

notes.html: One rule: WAF reads HTTP requests (URLs, headers, bodies). So it only attaches to services that speak HTTP (layer 7). Anything that just forwards TCP/UDP packets (layer 4) can't use it.

questions.q: A multiplayer game runs on EC2 behind NLBs in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 and uses UDP. Players worldwide report lag, and partner ISPs need exactly two fixed IP addresses to allowlist. What should the architect use?

options.t: CloudFront with both NLBs as origins
options.why: CloudFront only speaks HTTP/HTTPS/WebSocket. UDP can't go through it, and it has no static IPs.

options.t: Global Accelerator with an endpoint group in each region
options.why: Right. Any TCP/UDP, 2 static anycast IPs for the allowlist, and the AWS backbone cuts lag.

options.t: Route 53 latency-based routing to both NLBs
options.why: It picks a region but doesn't speed up the path, and it hands out the NLBs' IPs (several per region), not two fixed ones.

options.t: Elastic IPs on each NLB, published to the partners
options.why: That's at least one IP per AZ per region, not two, and traffic still crosses the public internet.

questions.q: A news site serves personalised HTML that can't be cached, plus images and CSS that can. All of it is HTTP from one ALB in us-east-1. Readers in Asia see slow pages. Which change has the least operational overhead?

options.t: Global Accelerator in front of the ALB
options.why: It would speed up the path, but it can't cache the images and CSS, so the origin keeps serving everything.

options.t: CloudFront with the ALB as origin: caching for static paths, TTL 0 for the HTML
options.why: Right. Static files come from the edge, and the dynamic HTML still gets edge TLS and the backbone. "Dynamic" doesn't rule CloudFront out.

options.t: Route 53 latency routing
options.why: There's only one region, so there's nothing to route between.

options.t: Deploy a copy of the stack in ap-southeast-1
options.why: It would work, but it's the most overhead (a second stack, data sync).

questions.q: A company does blue/green releases by shifting Route 53 weighted records. Its mobile app clients keep hitting the old (blue) stack for hours after the switch because they cache DNS. How do they make the switch take effect almost immediately?

options.t: Set the record TTL to 0
options.why: The clients are ignoring TTL already; that's the problem. A lower TTL doesn't fix clients that cache anyway.

options.t: Put Global Accelerator in front and shift traffic with endpoint weights / traffic dials
options.why: Right. Clients keep the same 2 anycast IPs; GA moves traffic behind them with no DNS change.

options.t: Switch to Route 53 failover routing
options.why: Still DNS, so it has the same caching problem.

options.t: Use a CloudFront origin group
options.why: Origin groups are for failover on errors, not planned traffic shifting, and only for GET/HEAD/OPTIONS.

questions.q: Product images in an S3 bucket get millions of GET requests a day from users worldwide. S3 request costs are high and far-away users see slow loads. What should the architect do?

options.t: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
options.why: It speeds up transfers to and from the bucket but caches nothing, so every GET still hits S3 and request costs stay the same.

options.t: Put CloudFront in front of the bucket with OAC
options.why: Right. CloudFront is the only one of these that caches. Fewer requests reach S3, and users are served from a nearby edge.

options.t: Put Global Accelerator in front of S3
options.why: GA doesn't cache, and S3 isn't a GA endpoint type.

options.t: Use Route 53 geolocation routing to buckets in several regions
options.why: That means replicating the data and adding overhead, and it still doesn't cache.

questions.q: An HTTPS payments API (mostly POST requests) runs active-passive in two regions. If the primary region fails, traffic must move within seconds, with no wait for DNS caches to expire. Which option meets this?

options.t: CloudFront with an origin group (primary + secondary region)
options.why: Origin failover only retries GET, HEAD and OPTIONS. POST requests would fail.

options.t: Route 53 failover routing with a 60-second TTL
options.why: Still DNS-based. Clients and resolvers can cache past the TTL.

options.t: Global Accelerator with an endpoint group per region
options.why: Right. GA health checks move traffic in seconds behind the same static IPs. It handles HTTPS (it's TCP) for any method.

options.t: Multivalue answer routing
options.why: DNS again, and it's for spreading load, not fast failover.

questions.q: A global shop needs product images cached near users AND SQL-injection attempts blocked before they reach its region. Which TWO should it use? (Choose TWO.)

options.t: CloudFront distribution in front of the ALB
options.why: Right. It caches the images at the edge.

options.t: AWS WAF web ACL on the CloudFront distribution
options.why: Right. WAF on CloudFront blocks bad requests at the edge, before they reach the region.

options.t: Global Accelerator
options.why: It doesn't cache, and WAF can't attach to it.

options.t: AWS WAF on a Network Load Balancer
options.why: WAF can't attach to an NLB.

options.t: Shield Standard on its own
options.why: Shield is for DDoS at layers 3/4. It doesn't inspect for SQL injection.

questions.q: By law, users in the EU must be served from eu-central-1. Everyone else goes to us-east-1. Which Route 53 setup meets this?

options.t: Latency-based routing
options.why: Latency picks the fastest region. An EU user on some networks could get us-east-1, which breaks the law.

options.t: Geolocation routing: Europe → eu-central-1, default → us-east-1
options.why: Right. Geolocation decides by where the user is. It's the policy for legal and content rules. Don't forget the default record.

options.t: Geoproximity routing with a bias toward eu-central-1
options.why: Geoproximity uses distance plus a bias, not country borders, so it can't guarantee the legal boundary.

options.t: Weighted routing 50/50
options.why: Random split, unrelated to location.

questions.q: An app runs in us-east-1, eu-west-1 and ap-northeast-1. The goal is the best response time for each user, decided at DNS level. Which policy?

options.t: Geolocation
options.why: Location isn't speed. The geographically closest region isn't always the fastest network path.

options.t: Latency-based
options.why: Right. Route 53 uses measured latency between user networks and AWS regions.

options.t: Geoproximity
options.why: That's for shifting traffic with a bias, not for measuring speed.

options.t: Multivalue answer
options.why: It returns several healthy IPs at random; it doesn't consider performance.

questions.q: Which statement about Route 53 geoproximity routing is correct today?

options.t: It only works if you create a Traffic Flow policy first
options.why: Outdated. Since 2024, geoproximity can be created as a normal record. Traffic Flow is optional.

options.t: It routes by the user's country, like geolocation
options.why: It uses the distance between user and resource, not country borders.

options.t: It's the only policy with a bias to grow or shrink a region's share of traffic, and it can be a normal record
options.why: Right. The bias dial is its unique feature, and Traffic Flow is no longer required.

options.t: It sends users to the region with the lowest measured latency
options.why: That's latency-based routing.

questions.q: A team wants to send 10% of users to a new version (green) and 90% to the current one (blue), then shift gradually. Users are web browsers that respect TTLs. Which is simplest?

options.t: Route 53 weighted records, 90/10, then shift the weights
options.why: Right. Weighted is the DNS answer for canaries and blue/green. Weight 0 stops traffic to a record.

options.t: Route 53 failover records
options.why: Failover is all-or-nothing on a health check, not a percentage split.

options.t: Geoproximity with a 10% bias
options.why: Bias shifts by distance, not by an exact percentage.

options.t: Global Accelerator
options.why: It works too, but it's more than needed since browsers respect DNS TTLs. The question asks for simplest.

questions.q: A company's main site runs behind an ALB. If the ALB becomes unhealthy, users should see a static "we'll be back soon" page hosted on S3. Which Route 53 setup?

options.t: Weighted records for the ALB and S3, both with health checks
options.why: That's active-active. S3 would get traffic even when the site is fine.

options.t: Failover routing: ALB as primary with a health check, S3 website as secondary
options.why: Right. Active-passive with a static fallback is the textbook use of the Failover policy.

options.t: Latency routing between the ALB and S3
options.why: Again active-active, and latency is the wrong criterion here.

options.t: Multivalue answer with both targets
options.why: Returns both while healthy, so users could land on the sorry page at random.

questions.q: An internal service lives in private subnets and is only resolvable through a private hosted zone. The team wants Route 53 to fail over when it becomes unhealthy. How do they health-check it?

options.t: Create an HTTP health check against the service's private IP
options.why: Route 53 health checkers run on the internet. They can't reach a private IP.

options.t: Create a CloudWatch alarm on the service's metric, and a Route 53 health check that monitors the alarm
options.why: Right. This is the standard pattern for private resources.

options.t: Open the security group to 0.0.0.0/0 so health checkers can reach it
options.why: It's still a private IP with no public route, and this would also be a security hole.

options.t: Use a calculated health check with no child checks
options.why: A calculated check needs child checks, and nothing here can reach the service.

questions.q: An architect proposes "Route 53 active-active failover routing" so two regions both serve traffic and an unhealthy one is dropped. What's wrong with that?

options.t: Nothing. That's a standard policy
options.why: There's no such policy. Failover routing is always active-passive.

options.t: Active-active is done with weighted, latency or multivalue records plus health checks, not the Failover policy
options.why: Right. Any policy except Failover, with health checks, gives active-active.

options.t: Active-active needs Global Accelerator; Route 53 can't do it
options.why: Route 53 can do active-active with health checks. GA is only needed for no-DNS failover or static IPs.

options.t: Active-active requires Aurora Global Database
options.why: That's the database layer. It has nothing to do with the DNS policy.

questions.q: example.com (the zone apex) must point at an Application Load Balancer. Which record?

options.t: CNAME example.com → the ALB's DNS name
options.why: CNAMEs aren't allowed at the zone apex.

options.t: A record with the ALB's current IP addresses
options.why: ALB IPs change. The record would break.

options.t: Alias A record → the ALB
options.why: Right. Alias works at the apex, follows the ALB's changing IPs, and queries are free.

options.t: MX record → the ALB
options.why: MX is for mail servers.

questions.q: A small company wants example.com (apex) to point at its single EC2 web server, which has an Elastic IP. What's the simplest, cheapest correct setup?

options.t: It's impossible without an ALB, because Alias can't target EC2
options.why: Wrong. Alias can't target EC2, but you don't need Alias here.

options.t: A record example.com → the Elastic IP
options.why: Right. A plain A record to a static IP works at the apex. No ALB needed.

options.t: CNAME example.com → the instance's public DNS name
options.why: No CNAMEs at the apex.

options.t: Alias record → the EC2 instance
options.why: EC2 instances aren't valid Alias targets.

questions.q: Users must upload files through a CloudFront distribution into an S3 bucket. The bucket must stay private, and no one may reach it except through CloudFront. What should the architect configure?

options.t: Make the bucket public-write and restrict by Referer header
options.why: Referer is trivial to fake, and the bucket would be public.

options.t: Origin Access Control (OAC), with the cache behavior allowing PUT/POST and a bucket policy for the distribution
options.why: Right. OAC is the current way to lock S3 to CloudFront, and it supports writes and SSE-KMS.

options.t: S3 Transfer Acceleration
options.why: Uploads would go to S3 directly, not through CloudFront, so the "only via CloudFront" rule breaks.

options.t: CloudFront geo restriction
options.why: It controls which countries can access. It doesn't keep the bucket private.

questions.q: Paying subscribers need access to every video under /premium/, and nobody else should get it. Videos are served by CloudFront. What's the cleanest approach?

options.t: A CloudFront signed URL per video
options.why: Works for one file, but it's clumsy for a whole area with hundreds of files.

options.t: CloudFront signed cookies
options.why: Right. One cookie grants access to many files, such as everything under /premium/.

options.t: S3 pre-signed URLs
options.why: These go to S3 directly and bypass CloudFront.

options.t: Geo restriction
options.why: That filters by country, not by who has paid.

questions.q: On every request, a site must add security headers and normalise URLs at the edge, at millions of requests per second, at the lowest cost. What fits best?

options.t: Lambda@Edge on viewer request
options.why: It works, but it costs more and scales lower. It's for heavier logic like auth calls or origin selection.

options.t: CloudFront Functions
options.why: Right. Sub-millisecond JavaScript at every edge location, made for header and URL tweaks at huge scale.

options.t: ALB listener rules
options.why: That runs in the region, not at the edge, and can't add response headers this way.

options.t: API Gateway mapping templates
options.why: Wrong layer, and it isn't in front of a CloudFront site.

questions.q: The origin ALB is in eu-west-1. The team wants a custom HTTPS domain on the CloudFront distribution using an ACM certificate. Where must the certificate be?

options.t: eu-west-1, the same region as the origin
options.why: A cert in eu-west-1 works on the ALB, not on CloudFront.

options.t: us-east-1
options.why: Right. CloudFront only uses ACM certificates from us-east-1, whatever the origin's region.

options.t: Any region; CloudFront is global
options.why: Global service, but the cert still has to live in us-east-1.

options.t: It must be imported into IAM
options.why: The IAM certificate store is legacy. ACM in us-east-1 is the answer.

questions.q: Which of these can AWS WAF NOT be attached to directly?

options.t: CloudFront distribution
options.why: Supported, and it's the best place: it blocks at the edge.

options.t: Application Load Balancer
options.why: Supported.

options.t: Network Load Balancer
options.why: Right. WAF is layer 7, and the NLB is layer 4. Protect the layer behind it, or use Shield Advanced for DDoS.

options.t: API Gateway REST API
options.why: Supported.

questions.q: A factory must run EC2 and EBS inside its own building with the same AWS APIs, because data can't leave the site.

options.t: AWS Outposts
options.why: AWS hardware in your data center.

options.t: Local Zones
options.why: AWS-run sites in cities, not your building.

options.t: Wavelength Zones
options.why: Inside telecom 5G networks.

options.t: Snowball Edge
options.why: Portable devices, not a long-term AWS footprint.

parts: A media company serves video worldwide
from an ALB in us-east-1.
Partners need to allowlist exactly two IP addresses
and users want lower latency.
items.why: "Two IP addresses" means static anycast IPs, which only GA gives you.

parts: A retailer runs in two regions.
Customers in Germany
must be served from eu-central-1 by law,
and everyone else from us-east-1.
items.why: "By law" means location rules, not speed. That's geolocation, not latency.

parts: A news site has global readers.
Article images are requested millions of times a day
and the team wants to reduce load on the origin
with minimal changes.
items.why: "Reduce load on the origin" means caching, and only CloudFront caches.

parts: A company's main site runs behind an ALB.
If it becomes unhealthy,
users should see a static maintenance page on S3.
Cost must stay low.
items.why: A static fallback page is the textbook active-passive pattern.

parts: A team runs blue/green releases with Route 53 weighted records,
but mobile clients cache DNS for hours,
so the switch is slow.
They want near-instant cut-over.
items.why: "Clients cache DNS" kills any DNS-based switch. GA moves traffic behind the same IPs.

parts: A team needs to move more users to a new region gradually
based on where users are, using a bias,
without changing their app.
items.why: "Bias" is the giveaway word. Only geoproximity has it.
